summary: This standards-track memo reserves a Mobile IPv4 message type, and related extension and error code space, for experimental use. It lets individuals or organisations try out enhancements to Mobile IPv4 before a formal proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: When inventors want to test new ideas, they need a spare slot that will not clash with real ones. This document sets aside a spare slot for Mobile IPv4.

questions: reserved experimental numbers in mobile ip
what is the mobile ipv4 experimental message type
what is a skippable extension in mobile ip
which mobile ip error codes are experimental
subtitle: Spare message, extension and error-code numbers in Mobile IPv4, set aside so experiments do not collide with real assignments.

tldr.problem: People who want to try out new Mobile IPv4 messages before a formal proposal would otherwise have to pick a value from the range IANA assigns, which can collide with real assignments.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves one message type (255), two extension types (127 non-skippable and 255 skippable, for both Mobile IPv4 and ICMP router discovery) and two error codes (127 for the foreign agent and 192 for the home agent) for experimental use, with an opaque payload.
tldr.outcome: Experiments get safe numbers, but experimental messages MUST be authenticated and experimental extensions should not be used in deployed products. A successful experiment should get a permanent number from IANA.

today: RFC 4064 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2005. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it relies on the base Mobile IPv4 specification in RFC 3344.

sections.title: Why Reserve Experimental Numbers
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 message types range from 0 to 255. Without a reserved experimental message, someone testing an enhancement would have to pick a type from the range defined for IANA assignment, which may result in collisions.

Mobile IP also has a general extension mechanism for optional information in control messages. Extensions in the range 0 to 127 are not skippable, and those in the range 128 to 255 are skippable. Error codes are defined for the foreign agent (FA) in 64 to 127 and for the home agent (HA) in 128 to 192. This RFC reserves extension types in both extension ranges and one error code in each error range.

The reservations follow Section 2.2 of BCP 82, RFC 3692. The base protocol is RFC 3344.
sections.plainLanguage: Real numbers are like seats in a theatre that are already booked. This document keeps a few seats free for people who are only trying things out.

sections.title: The Reserved Values
sections.content:
The RFC names each reserved value and says which number IANA assigned.

  • EXP-MSG-TYPE: message type 255.
  • EXP-SKIP-EXT-TYPE: skippable extension 255, used in Mobile IPv4 and in ICMP router discovery Agent Advertisement.
  • EXP-NONSKIP-EXT-TYPE: non-skippable extension 127, used in the same two places.
  • EXP-HA-ERROR-CODE: error code 192, for the HA in reply messages.
  • EXP-FA-ERROR-CODE: error code 127, for the FA in reply messages.

The mobility entities are the home agent, foreign agent and mobile node.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one spare message number, two spare add-on numbers and two spare error numbers, and each one has a name so people can talk about it.

sections.title: The Experimental Message
sections.content:
Because the purpose of an experimental message cannot be known in advance, its structure is an opaque payload. Entities that implement it interpret it as they choose; one suggestion is to interpret it based on the extensions it carries. It may be used between the home agent, foreign agent and mobile node, and it MAY contain Mobile IP extensions, including vendor-specific ones.

Like other Mobile IP control messages, it travels over UDP with destination port 434. After the UDP header comes a Type field of 255 followed by zero or more octets of opaque data.

Experimental messages MUST be authenticated with one of the authentication mechanisms defined for Mobile IP. Once an experiment has been tested and shown to be useful, a permanent number should be obtained through the normal IANA procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The experimental message is a sealed envelope with a fixed label on the outside. Whatever is inside is up to whoever is running the experiment.

sections.title: Experimental Extensions
sections.content:
There are four extension formats. Mobile IPv4 uses the long extension format for non-skippable extensions and the short format for skippable ones, as defined in RFC 3344.

  • Non-skippable Mobile IPv4 (Type 127): fields Type, Sub-Type, a 16-bit Length and opaque data. Because the length field is 16 bits wide, the data can exceed 256 bytes.
  • Skippable Mobile IPv4 (Type 255): Type, an 8-bit Length, Sub-Type and opaque data. The RFC says the data cannot exceed 256 bytes.
  • Non-skippable ICMP router discovery (Type 127): Type, Length and opaque data, with no Sub-Type. A node that does not recognize it should ignore it.
  • Skippable ICMP router discovery (Type 255): Type, Length and opaque data. It should be ignored if the implementation does not understand it.

Sub-Type is a unique number given to each member of the aggregated type. Length never includes the Type (and Sub-Type, where present) and Length fields.
sections.plainLanguage: An extension is a small sticky note attached to a message. Some notes can be ignored if you do not understand them, and others mean you must not accept the message at all.

sections.title: Experimental Error Codes
sections.content:
The FA may use code 127 and the HA may use code 192 in registration reply messages. It is recommended that experimental error codes be used with experimental messages and extensions whenever none of the standardized error codes apply.

Foreign agents and home agents SHOULD include an experimental error code in a reply only if they have a general indication that the receiver can parse it. That is the case when the request was of type EXP-MSG-TYPE or contained at least one experimental extension.
sections.plainLanguage: If an experiment goes wrong in a way no ordinary error covers, the agents have a spare error number to say so. They only use it when the other side is in on the experiment.

sections.title: Behavior of Mobility Entities
sections.content:
Implementations that do not understand the experimental message type SHOULD silently discard it. Entities that do not understand skippable experimental extensions MUST ignore them. If they do not understand a non-skippable experimental extension, they MUST silently discard the whole message containing it, consistent with Section 1.8 of RFC 3344.

Experimental extensions can ride in experimental messages and in standards-defined messages. In the latter case the RFC suggests that experimental extensions MUST NOT be used in deployed products and that use be restricted to experiments only.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone does not know about your experiment, they either ignore your sticky note or throw the whole letter away, depending on how important the note said it was.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Like all Mobile IP control messages, experimental messages MUST be authenticated per the requirements of RFC 3344 or the second authentication reference the RFC cites. Experimental messages without a valid authenticator SHOULD be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a test message has to show proof of who sent it, or it gets thrown away.
